opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting and also one of the most honestly uncertain areas right now. The short answer is that it's very promising, but it depends heavily on how close your robot and your task are to what the base model has already seen.

When we were working on things like RT-1 and RT-2, and then the cross-embodiment efforts like Open X-Embodiment, one of the clearest lessons was that pre-training on large, diverse data gives you a much better starting point. If you take a model that's seen hundreds of thousands of episodes across many robots and environments, and you fine-tune it on your setup, you often need far fewer demonstrations than if you trained from scratch. Instead of thousands of demos, you might get somewhere useful with tens or maybe a couple hundred, depending on the task.

But "a few demonstrations" covers a wide range. If your robot is a fairly standard arm, say a parallel-jaw gripper with a wrist camera and a third-person view, and your task is a variation on pick-and-place, you're in good shape. The model already has a strong prior on what grasping looks like, how objects move, what language instructions map to. Fine-tuning there is mostly about calibrating to your camera angles, your action space, your control frequency.

Where it gets harder is when you move away from that distribution. A very different embodiment, like a dexterous hand, a mobile manipulator, or something with unusual kinematics, or a task that needs precise force control, contact-rich manipulation, or long-horizon reasoning. There the pre-trained model helps less, and a handful of demos often isn't enough to get robust behavior. You might get something that works in the exact conditions you demoed, but it's brittle when lighting changes, objects move a few centimeters, or a distractor shows up.

So when I assess it, I look at a few things. How similar is the observation space, meaning the cameras, viewpoints, and resolution? How similar is the action space, since end-effector control transfers much better than joint control across robots? How much does the task rely on semantic understanding, which these models are good at, versus fine-grained physical skill, which still mostly comes from your own data? And how will you evaluate it? A lot of the few-shot results you see look great on a curated set of trials, and the real test is whether it holds up over hundreds of attempts with natural variation.

My honest take is that we're at the point where few-shot adaptation is real and practically useful, especially for research labs and for fairly constrained industrial settings. But we're not yet at the point where you can unbox a new robot, show it five times, and get production-level reliability. The gap is mostly data diversity on the physical side. Vision-language models had the whole internet; robotics doesn't have that, so the community is still building the equivalent. As that grows, and as action representations get more standardized across embodiments, I expect the number of demos you need to keep dropping pretty dramatically.

r001.rationale: The response says a few demonstrations may help on familiar tasks, but it does not connect strong performance to repeatable hardware; it also says five demonstrations are not enough for production-level reliability.

r002.rationale: It says behavior can be brittle when lighting, object positions, or distractors vary, and that a handful of demonstrations may not yield robust behavior outside the demonstrated conditions.

r003.rationale: It identifies precise force control, contact-rich manipulation, and long-horizon reasoning as harder cases where a handful of demonstrations often is not enough for robust behavior.

r004.rationale: It describes fine-tuning a pre-trained model on the user's setup as a way to adapt it, using data from that setup.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's really the whole promise of a robotics foundation model, right? The dream is that you take a model that's been trained on a huge amount of diverse robot data, and then you show up with your own robot, your own gripper, your own kitchen or warehouse or lab bench, and you give it maybe ten, twenty, fifty demonstrations and it just works.

I'd say we're partway there, and I want to be honest about which parts are real and which are still aspirational.

The part that's real is that pretraining genuinely helps. When we trained RT-2 on top of a vision-language model, the thing that surprised a lot of people was the emergent generalization. The robot could handle objects it had never been trained to manipulate, follow instructions with concepts it had only seen in web data, do a bit of reasoning about which object is the right one. That transfer comes from the language and vision backbone, and it means that when you fine-tune on your task, you're not starting from zero. You're starting from a model that already understands what a cup is, what "pick up" means, roughly how objects behave.

Then with RT-X and the Open X-Embodiment effort, we specifically tested cross-embodiment transfer. Data from many different robots, different labs, different action spaces, pooled together. And the headline result was that a model trained on that pooled data outperformed models trained on any single robot's data, including on that robot's own tasks. So diversity of embodiment in pretraining actually helps you on a new embodiment. That's the encouraging piece for someone with their own robot.

Now the honest caveats. First, the few-shot story works best when your robot is not too far from the distribution. If you have a standard arm with a parallel-jaw gripper and a wrist camera, you're in good shape. If you have a very unusual morphology, a soft gripper, a humanoid hand, a very different camera placement, the gap is bigger, and you'll need more data or a careful adaptation strategy for the action space. Action representation is genuinely one of the hardest parts of cross-embodiment transfer and it's still not solved.

Second, "a few demonstrations" means different things depending on the task. For a short-horizon pick-and-place where the hard part is perception and grounding, tens of demos can be enough because the pretrained model has already done most of the work. For a long-horizon, contact-rich task where precise force control matters, fifty demos is not going to get you to high reliability. The pretrained model doesn't have strong priors about your specific dynamics.

Third, and this is the thing people underestimate, the quality and coverage of those few demonstrations matters enormously. If all your demos are from the same starting position with the same object, you've shown the model one thing, not a task. Variety across a small number of demos is worth far more than many near-identical ones.

So my overall assessment is that adaptation with few demonstrations is real and improving fast, especially for the perception and semantic understanding parts of the problem. Where it's still weak is low-level control on novel embodiments and precision on hard manipulation. And I think the path forward is partly more and more diverse pretraining data, so that more robots fall "in distribution," and partly better ways of representing actions so that the model can transfer motor skill, not just understanding, across bodies. We're not fully there yet, but the trend line is very clear.

r001.rationale: It says a standard arm with a parallel-jaw gripper and wrist camera is a good fit, but does not connect few demonstrations and strong performance to repeatable hardware.

r002.rationale: It stresses that demonstration variety and coverage matter, but does not state that working across a broader range of situations requires more demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It says fifty demonstrations will not deliver high reliability for difficult contact-rich tasks, but does not clearly state that harder tasks require more demonstrations.

r004.rationale: It describes a pretrained robotics model being fine-tuned on the user's task, after the user provides demonstrations for their own robot.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction. But the important question is: what does the model already know before you give it those few demonstrations? If it has learned useful representations and behaviors from a broad range of robotics data, then a small number of demonstrations could help specify your task or adapt a familiar behavior to your setup.

Adapting to a different robot can be a bigger challenge. The camera placement, the gripper, the action space—all of those can change. So learning a new task on a robot the model already understands is different from learning that task on an entirely new embodiment.

I’m optimistic about using a few demonstrations to adapt pretrained models, but I’d distinguish getting an encouraging rollout from getting reliable performance. You want to know whether it still works when the object moves, when the initial conditions change, or when something goes wrong and the robot has to recover. That’s the standard that makes this practically useful.

r001.rationale: The response says a few demonstrations may help adapt a pretrained model, but does not connect strong performance to repeatable hardware.

r002.rationale: It mentions varying conditions as a reliability standard, but does not state that broader coverage requires more demonstrations.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that harder tasks require more demonstration data.

r004.rationale: It discusses adapting pretrained models with a few demonstrations, but does not identify fine-tuning a shared model with a user's specialized data as a way to adapt it to that user's robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s one of the most exciting possibilities for robotics foundation models. If you’re starting from a model that has already learned a broad range of behaviors, a few demonstrations can potentially tell it what you want to do, rather than having to teach it every aspect of how to move and interact with the world from scratch.

But I’d separate adapting to a new task from adapting to a new robot. If the robot and environment are similar to what the model has seen before, a few demonstrations might be enough to adapt a behavior. If you’re changing the embodiment—the sensors, the action space, the way the robot moves—that’s a much bigger challenge. You need some way to connect the model’s prior experience to this new hardware.

So I’m optimistic, but the important question is how much variation those few demonstrations have to cover. Getting a successful execution is one thing. Getting a policy that reliably handles different starting conditions, mistakes, and unexpected situations is another. The promise is that pretraining supplies that broader experience, so your demonstrations can focus on the specifics of your task.

r001.rationale: The response says a few demonstrations might adapt behavior when the robot and environment are similar, but does not state that repeatable hardware enables strong robotics performance.

r002.rationale: It discusses covering variation and handling unexpected situations, but does not clearly state that a broader range of situations requires more demonstration data.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect task difficulty to the amount of demonstration data needed.

r004.rationale: It discusses adapting a model to new hardware, but does not identify fine-tuning a shared robotics model with the user’s specialized data as a possible approach.
